name: FFmpeg ffvp9 (libavcodec VP9 decoder)
baseline: libvpx VP9 decoder (libvpx-vp9, Google's reference decoder)
workload: Software decode time of VP9 clips (Sintel, Tears of Steel, Enter the Void) encoded to matching SSIM, measured as user time of `ffmpeg -threads 1 [-c:v libvpx-vp9] -i $file -f null` with ffvp9 versus libvpx-vp9 as the decoder.
claimed_speedup: ffvp9 is 25-50% faster than libvpx's VP9 decoder on a variety of machines (Phoronix summary of the February 2014 post by Ronald Bultje); ffvp9 also scales across threads where libvpx's multithreading is described as nearly useless; Phoronix 2017 coverage: ffvp9 tile threading about 25% faster than libvpx-vp9 at two threads.
stars_or_usage: 65.0k stars on the GitHub mirror; used by most open-source media players and browsers
tradeoffs: Decode only; the encoder for VP9 is libvpx or other external libraries. The library is LGPL-2.1-or-later and becomes GPL when GPL components are enabled. ffvp9 tile and frame threading scales differently from ffh264.
caveats: Snippet only: the blog post, Phoronix, Slashdot and Wikipedia pages could not be opened in this session (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND), so the numbers come from WebSearch result text. The post is first-party (an FFmpeg developer measuring his own decoder). Command line and clips are stated, but CPU models, compiler and flags were not captured, so this is tier C. Data are from 2014, and libvpx later gained AVX2 and better multithreading; an FFmpeg developer IRC log from January 2016 (snippet) said the gap on Haswell was smaller. Wikipedia repeats the 25-50% figure for 2016 (snippet, not opened). FFmpeg as a whole is a large multimedia suite; this record documents only the VP9 decoder component.
